Sheriff's deputies in Washington County, Idaho, arrested Randy Vail near Cambridge, Idaho, in connection with shooting attacks that damaged power substations at Hells Canyon and Brownlee dams. Vail subsequently faced both state and federal charges in connection with the attacks, though the state charges were later dropped in favor of the federal prosecution. According to authorities, Vail was motivated by anti-government and anti-law enforcement beliefs, and claimed that the government was illegitimate and that he did not recognize its authority. He also said that he wanted to "make a statement" and wanted a revolution or civil war. In June 2024, following a March plea deal in which he pleaded guilty to destruction of an energy facility, Vail was sentenced to five years of probation and ordered to pay $550,000 in restitution for the damage he caused.

Two corrections officers were injured. Authorities say that during their time at large, the escapees killed two men, one 83 years old and the other 72 years old, both on the same day. In an international terrorist incident, federal authorities arrested a Pakistani citizen, Asif Merchant, in connection with an alleged plot to conduct political assassinations in the United States. Merchant allegedly traveled to New York in April 2024 to hire hitmen to carry out the killings, but ended up paying a $5,000 advance to undercover law enforcement officers posing as potential assassins. Federal authorities say that Merchant had ties to Iran. He was charged with one count of murder for hire, but in September 2024 federal prosecutors filed a new indictment that also charged him with attempting to carry out an act of terrorism.

In August 2024, federal authorities charged Hashem Younis Hashem Hnaihen, a Jordanian, with destruction of an energy facility and four counts of threatening to use explosives. According to prosecutors, Hnaihen sought to target businesses that he believed were supportive of Israel. Beginning in June 2024, he vandalized several businesses and facilities, including a propane gas distribution depot, leaving "warning letters" at the premises that included threats and demands. Hnaihen also allegedly attacked a solar power facility, causing more than $700,000 in damage. Hnaihen pleaded guilty in December 2024 to four counts of threatening to use explosives and one count of destruction of an energy facility.

As part of a two-country investigation, Canadian authorities arrested a Pakistani citizen, Muhammad Shahzeb Khan, while trying to cross the border into the United States, allegedly as part of a planned mass shooting against a Jewish target in Brooklyn in order to support the extremist group ISIS. According to authorities, Khan boasted that his attack would be the "largest attack on U.S. soil since 9/11." A federal indictment in the Southern District of New York charged Khan with one count of attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

Federal authorities arrested two leaders of the online white supremacist group known as the Terrorgram Collective, notorious for its support of hate crimes and terrorism, on numerous charges, including solicitation of murder of a federal official, solicitation of a hate crime and conspiracy to provide material support for terrorism. Arrested were Dallas Erin Humber and Matthew Robert Allison.

Ryan Wesley Routh was arrested by police following an incident at a golf course in south Florida in which he was apparently planning to shoot former president Donald Trump, who was playing golf on that course that day. Routh allegedly had a rifle and scope with him at the time. According to authorities, he left a note with a friend in which he acknowledged his intention to assassinate the former president. A former Trump supporter who had seemingly become disillusioned with the ex-president, Routh had views that were all over the political map. He spoke in favor of both Democratic and Republican politicians and in a 2023 self-published book claimed that he "refused to be put in a category" such as Democrat or Republican. Routh was a strong supporter of the war in Ukraine and had even tried to solicit volunteers to fight against the Russian invasion of that country. Online posts by Routh suggested that in recent years he had become anti-Trump.

Federal authorities arrested Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, an Afghan citizen, charging him with plotting a mass casualty attack in the U.S. on Election Day. Tawhedi had allegedly associated himself with the terrorist group ISIS-K. The arrest was part of a sting operation in which Tawhedi allegedly purchased two assault rifles and ammunition from an undercover informant. Prosecutors said that Tawhedi had an accomplice, a teenaged relative, whom they have not named. Another family member was subsequently arrested in France, charged there with plotting to conduct terror attacks in that country. Tawhedi has been charged with conspiring and attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State.

Police in Arizona arrested a teenager on state charges of terrorism and conspiracy to commit terrorism, alleging that he had been inspired by the terrorist group ISIS to plot an attack on a Phoenix Pride parade using a remote-controlled drone with explosives. Deputies who responded to a disturbance call on August 2, 2024, were met with gunfire at the back door of a home. Two of the deputies were injured and a third killed. According to law enforcement, the suspects?two parents and two adult children?had stockpiled guns and ammunition, as well as food and supplies, and had anti-government propaganda and "conspiracy-theory media" inside the home. Statements made by the suspects also indicate they had religious beliefs. The sheriff's office said that the mother attempted to lure her neighbors, whom she believed were pedophiles, into a fatal ambush in the home, but when law enforcement arrived, she convinced them to enter the home instead. The father opened fire when the deputies entered. The mother, Julie Sulpizio, was arrested on suspicion of murder, attempted murder and other charges. Her husband, Michael Sulpizio, and two adult daughters, Savannah and Cheyenne Sulpizio, died inside the home, apparently killing themselves after the ambush.

On August 29, 2024, Corey Cobb-Bey, a sovereign citizen and Moorish Science Temple adherent, pulled his vehicle near a parked police cruiser, then got out and approached the officer sitting in the cruiser. After a brief discussion, Cobb-Bey pulled out a gun and shot the officer at point-blank range, killing him. Cobb-Bey removed a shotgun from the police cruiser, then waited for other officers to respond to the killing, engaging them in gunfire when they arrived and wounding two officers, one of whom was shot in the face and permanently blinded by her injuries. Cobb-Bey then fled in his own vehicle. After a 20-mile chase, he stopped, exiting his vehicle with a shotgun that he pointed at officers exiting their own vehicles; he died after multiple officers fired at him. Police have characterized the incident as an "ambush" and "execution."

On July 15, 2020, Freddie Lewis Tilton and five other people kidnapped a man with whom Tilton was having a dispute over a trailer. They took him to a residence, beat and tortured him, then shot and killed him. Tilton has a tattoo indicating he is an individual associated with the Joplin Honkeys, an active Missouri-based white supremacist prison gang; there is evidence to suggest some of the other kidnappers may also have been individuals associated with the group. After a tip led Newton County deputies to Tilton's residence, he fired shots at them before a SWAT team used tear gas to force him out of the building and arrested him. Federal prosecutors indicted six people; all defendants eventually pleaded guilty to various charges, receiving sentences that ranged up to 30 years. As of this writing, however, it appears that Tilton has not yet been sentenced.

Yellowstone National Park rangers shot and killed Samson Fussner as he shot at a ranger who spotted him approaching the Canyon Village dining facility for park employees. They were on the lookout for Fussner after he held a woman hostage for several hours the night before. Authorities believe Fussner, who had made white supremacist and antisemitic comments both to his hostage and online, intended to conduct mass shootings at the dining facility and a Fourth of July fireworks display.

Shamsud-Din Jabbar bypassed barriers to drive a rental truck into a crowd of New Year's celebrators on Bourbon Street in New Orleans, an attack that left 15 people dead and dozens more injured. The suspect, who reportedly made videos prior to the attack in which he claimed to have joined the Islamic extremist group ISIS, had an ISIS flag on his vehicle. He also had firearms, which he allegedly used to shoot at people as he drove through the crowd. Jabbar died in a shootout with law enforcement officers responding to the attack. Shortly afterwards police found explosive devices in the vicinity of the attack, possibly intended to target first responders. The FBI has said it believes Jabbar had accomplices; the investigation is still ongoing.

After the arson of one police vehicle, an online post took credit for the attack that read: "In solidarity with our Palestinian siblings assaulted by the Zionist state in Rafah."

Federal agents arrested Andrew Takhistov at Newark Liberty International Airport, charging him with soliciting the destruction of energy facilities. The 18-year-old white supremacist allegedly taught an undercover law enforcement officer how to attack electrical substations in New Jersey. Takhistov, who had made arrangements to travel to Ukraine to fight with a far right combat group of Russian volunteers, also allegedly hoped to be able to bring back illegal materials from Ukraine in order to launch attacks in the United States. He reportedly said that his "ultimate dream" was to use a rocket to attack a synagogue.

He was arrested in Moldova to be extradited to the United States. Chkhikvishvili allegedly was an individual associated with the Maniac Murder Cult, one of several mostly-online and loosely-organized groups that combine elements of white supremacy, accelerationism, the occult and a penchant for demonstrative violence. According to authorities, he attempted to recruit others, including an undercover law enforcement officer, to commit a mass casualty attack in New York City. He also allegedly encouraged bombings, arsons and poisonings against Jews, racial minorities and homeless people.

Sebolt has a lengthy criminal history. A woman present at the scene later identified Sebolt as the shooter. Sebolt was charged with and convicted of murder; in December 2024, he was sentenced to 60 years in prison. The woman has also been charged with murder but has not been tried as of this writing.

Early on February 11, Kevin Colantonio set fires outside a predominantly Black church. Though the building was damaged, responders arrived quickly enough to prevent the church from being destroyed. Colantonio was subsequently arrested for the arson. Investigating officers found a notebook containing racist and extreme writings, including phrases such as "Gun down everyone that isn't white" and "Always give our bloodline a chance" as well as language about burning churches. In December 2024, Colantonio admitted to the crime, pleading guilty to several charges, including a federal hate crime charge.

Police arrested Mack Adams Davis following an incident in which he fired shots at parked vehicles in his neighborhood. A subsequent investigation revealed that Davis had actually been plotting to commit mass shootings at a local Democratic Party headquarters and an LGBTQ+ bar because he associated both targets with the LGBTQ+ community and had accumulated an arsenal of weapons and ammunition with which to conduct the attacks. Police also found writings federal prosecutors later described as "indicating a support for Nazi ideology," including a notebook with a swastika and antisemitic statements, as well as anti-LGBTQ+ language. According to authorities, Davis frequently wrote about plans to conduct mass shootings against synagogues, mosques and other targets. In December 2024, Davis pleaded guilty to federal hate crimes charges, admitting he plotted to conduct an anti-LGBTQ+ mass killing.

On August 6, Zachary Babitz allegedly shot and killed an 83-year-old man outside a Best Buy store in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He then drove south in the victim's vehicle to Las Cruces, where he and a woman allegedly robbed a fast food restaurant and carjacked a vehicle. Babitz was subsequently apprehended. Babitz has a "1488" tattooed on his fingers and prior to the killing had recently become associated with the white supremacist Asatru Folk Assembly. Federal prosecutors charged Babitz with carjacking and related crimes. Initially, state prosecutors had charged Babitz as well but they dropped those charges in order to participate in the federal prosecution.

Montana authorities arrested Daren Christopher Abbey, a self-described white supremacist with a prior hate crime conviction and multiple white supremacist tattoos, for the alleged murder of a man camping in a tent near Big Sky in southwestern Montana on October 10, 2024. He was charged with deliberate homicide and tampering with evidence. The motive for the killing is not clear. Abbey claimed self-defense, though he allegedly admitted to removing evidence from the crime scene and taking items belonging to the victim. Police say Abbey admitted to assaulting the victim with multiple items, including a screwdriver and an axe.

In a sting operation, FBI agents arrested an accelerationist white supremacist, Skyler Philippi, charging him with attempting to use a weapon of mass destruction and attempting to destroy an energy facility. According to authorities, Philippi originally expressed interest to a confidential source in committing a mass shooting, then gravitated towards attacking the electrical grid. He allegedly planned to attach explosives to a drone and fly it into an electrical substation. However, the explosives had been provided by an undercover FBI agent and were inert. He was arrested while trying to launch the drone.

White supremacist fugitive Daniel Meinhart was shot by members of a U.S. Marshals Service Violent Fugitive Apprehension Strike Team who were attempting to arrest him. Meinhart, a documented member of Soldiers of Aryan Culture, a white supremacist prison gang, has an extensive criminal history including a conviction of attempted murder of a sheriff's deputy in 2003.

Cole allegedly set fire to the home of a relative following a child custody dispute. A car chase ensued when police arrived on the scene; according to authorities, Cole crashed his vehicle into another vehicle, killing one of its occupants and seriously injuring two others.

Following a tip from the suspect's family, law enforcement officers arrested Forrest Pemberton of Gainesville, Florida, following a traffic stop during which they allegedly found multiple firearms in his vehicle. Pemberton was subsequently charged by federal authorities with stalking with the intent to kill, injure, harass, intimidate or surveil. Authorities say he intended to travel to the south Florida offices of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel advocacy group, with the intent of harming people there, possibly in a suicide attack. According to the Gainesville Police Department, Pemberton "often cited extreme rightwing neo-Nazi type statements and has shown anti-authority tendencies."

Anderson Lee Aldrich was charged with 5 counts of first degree murder, 86 counts of attempted first degree murder, 48 counts of bias crimes and 90 counts of assault for a November 19, 2022, shooting spree against an LGBT+ nightclub. He was also charged federally with 74 hate crime and firearms counts. Aldrich appears to have tried but failed to livestream the deadly attack. Some months before the attack, Aldrich had created a small 4chan-like website in which he "showcased" an accelerationist white supremacist video called "Wrong Target," the purpose of which was to convince people to launch violent attacks against Jews, non-whites and other targets. In June 2023, following a guilty plea to the state charges, Aldrich received a sentence of five consecutive life sentences plus an additional 2,211 years in prison. In June 2024, following a guilty plea on the federal charges, Aldrich was sentenced to multiple life sentences plus 190 years in prison.

On October 26, Sidi Mohamed Abdallahi allegedly shot a Jewish man walking to his synagogue on a Saturday morning. When police and paramedics arrived on the scene shortly after the shooting, Abdallahi reportedly came out of an alleyway to open fire on them. Police returned fire, injuring and disabling the suspect, who was subsequently arrested. A door camera recording allegedly showed the shooter yelling, "Allahu Akbar" as he began to shoot at police. The suspect was originally charged with six counts of attempted murder, seven counts of aggravated discharge of a firearm and aggravated battery. At the end of the month, local authorities also filed felony hate crime and terrorism charges against Abdallahi, saying that evidence from his phone indicated that the suspect planned the shooting and intentionally sought to target Jews. Abdallahi committed suicide in his jail cell in December 2024.

On July 19, 2021, Rene Ayarde, a home health aide, murdered an 80-year-old man for whom she was caring, bludgeoning him to death and writing on his chest that read: "I touch little girls." Ayarde, her 3-year-old daughter and her mother shared an apartment with the victim. Ayarde claimed that the victim was a "devil worshipper" and had sexually abused her daughter, though when police encountered Ayarde she herself was physically abusing the young girl. Ayarde told police that she was a sovereign citizen and that they had no jurisdiction over her. She was charged with child abuse and murder; in January 2024 she pleaded guilty to a lesser count of manslaughter, later receiving a 14-year prison sentence.

John Jay Niebuhr, who was associated with the anti-government sovereign citizen ideology, was shot and killed by police after he attempted to drive his vehicle through a secure gate on the perimeter of the Melbourne Orlando International Airport and threatened approaching officers with a weapon. Prior to this incident, the Palm Bay Police Department had distributed a "situational awareness bulletin" about Niebuhr to its officers that described his previous encounters with police and his claim to be a sovereign citizen.

Prosecutors charged Nathanial James McGuire on numerous counts after he allegedly set off an improvised explosive device at a California courthouse. Six people suffered minor injuries. After the bombing, McGuire allegedly shouted that the government had taken his guns and people needed to rise up and rebel. In a video of his arrest posted to social media, McGuire allegedly called people traitors and told them not to violate the Constitution. When police searched his car, they reportedly discovered more firearms, another explosive device and ten Molotov cocktails. McGuire had previously been arrested in July after police allegedly seized a loaded concealed but unregistered handgun; he was scheduled to be arraigned on the day of the bombing. In October, federal prosecutors charged McGuire with using a weapon of mass destruction and other charges.

In the body-cam footage released by police, Clark mentioned several times how he was "not operating in commerce," a common sovereign citizen refrain.

An FBI sting operation following a tip about bombmaking resulted in the arrest of Harun Abdul-Malik Yener on charges related to an alleged plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). According to authorities, in 2015 Yener considered going to Iraq to join the terrorist group ISIS, but he ultimately decided not to. In subsequent years, his interests gravitated towards far-right groups and movements, such as the Proud Boys and the anti-government boogaloo and militia movements. Yener allegedly told an FBI confidential source that he'd unsuccessfully attempted to join the Proud Boys and boogaloos, but they rejected him because he had wanted to pursue "martyrdom." The FBI used undercover agents to pose as members of a militia group to investigate his desire for a "reboot" or "revolution" in the country. Yener allegedly settled on the NYSE as a target because people would be sympathetic to an attack on it and it would "wake people up." Yener has been charged with attempted use of an explosive to damage or destroy a building used in interstate commerce.

Miner was angry at Moreno for allegedly selling fake drugs to a friend of his. In 2024, Miner pleaded guilty to one count of felony murder and received a 30-year sentence.

Larry Edward Foxworth, a self-described white supremacist, conducted an attempted shooting spree from a vehicle against two convenience stores in an Atlanta suburb. Both stores had customers and staff inside when attacked, but luckily no one was hit. After his arrest, Foxworth confessed that he shot at the stores in an attempt to kill Black and Arab people. Foxworth subsequently pleaded guilty to federal hate crime charges; the agreement calls for a sentence of 20 to 25 years in prison.

Alerted by the FBI, police arrested a teenager livestreaming a video in which he allegedly announced he was going to kill his father and take his van, then shoot at black people before conducting a mass shooting at a synagogue. Police found two handguns which had racist and antisemitic symbols and messages on them, as well as a document variously described as a journal and a manifesto. The teen admitted to police that he was a white supremacist. He has been charged with terrorist threats, domestic violence, inducing panic and threatening violence and possessing criminal tools. Police believe the teenager was perhaps only minutes or hours away from carrying out his threats.

Coby Dale Green broke the glass door of a donut shop and threw a Molotov cocktail into the business. The incendiary device did not fully erupt but did cause fire damage. The subsequent investigation revealed Green's anti-LGBTQ+ activities, as well as social media posts attacking the donut shop for its association with drag queens. Green was charged with and later pleaded guilty to malicious use of explosives. He received a five-year federal prison sentence.

A grand jury in New York City indicted Matthew Mahrer and Christopher Brown on conspiracy, threat and weapons charges following their arrest on November 19 as they tried to enter Penn Station with firearms, bulletproof vests and masks. Police suspect the pair were plotting to conduct a shooting at a synagogue. One of the two suspects, Brown, allegedly has had a long history of white supremacist online postings.

Authorities arrested a Canadian citizen, Cameron Monte Smith, following a shooting attack against an electrical substation in May 2023; the subsequent investigation revealed that Smith had also been responsible for a similar shooting attack at a transformer and pump station for the Keystone Pipeline in July 2022. The shootings together caused around $1.7 million in damage. The letters "DAPL" and other symbols were found spray-painted near the substation; "DAPL" stands for Dakota Access Pipeline, a controversial pipeline opposed by far-left activists. In September 2024, Smith pleaded guilty to two counts of destruction of an energy facility.

According to authorities, Said sought to engage in violence either by traveling abroad to help the Islamic terrorist group ISIS or by attacking a target in the U.S. They also said he planned a mass shooting at the U.S. Army's Tank-Automotive and Armaments Command facility near Detroit and had even conducted surveillance on the target using a drone.

Cameron Smith, a Canadian citizen, used a high-powered rifle to shoot up an electrical transformer and pump station for the Keystone Pipeline near Carpenter, South Dakota, causing substantial damage. On May 13, 2023, he similarly attacked an electrical substation near Ray, North Dakota, also causing substantial damage. In court, Smith said he was frustrated after years of unsuccessfully trying to raise awareness of climate change through lawful means. Smith pleaded guilty to destroying energy facilities and illegally possessing a firearm and ammunition, and in March 2025, a federal judge sentenced him to 25 years in prison.

Capitol Police officers arrested Riley Jane English (also known as Ryan Michael English) after she turned herself in at the Capitol, admitting to police that she had driven from Massachusetts to kill Scott Bessent, the nominee to be Donald Trump's Treasury Secretary, who was there for his confirmation. She allegedly had a knife and two Molotov cocktails in her possession at the time. In May 2025, federal prosecutors indicted her on charges of carrying a dangerous weapon or incendiary device on Capitol grounds and unlawful possession of an incendiary device. English had allegedly considered several targets before finally settling on Bessent. However, she turned herself in after allegedly finding security at the Capitol to be too tight. In a note she had with her at the time of her arrest, she wrote: "I can't do nothing while nazis kill my sisters." The reference to "sisters" may have been an allusion to women who were, like English, transgender.

Graffiti equating ICE with the Ku Klux Klan was also found on the outside of the building. Authorities say Wagner was responsible for an earlier arson of vehicles at a local Tesla dealership in February, as well as graffiti that read: "Die Tesla Nazi" and "Tesla Nazi Inc." Federal prosecutors have charged Wagner with two counts of malicious damage or destruction of property by fire or explosives.

Federal authorities arrested Jakhi Lodgson McCray in July 2025 for a June 12 arson in Brooklyn, alleging that he climbed a fence to get into a parking lot and set fire to 10 police vehicles, causing more than $800,000 in damage. In a statement McCray released after his arrest, he criticized the "brutality of state repression" and the "kidnapping of migrants." McCray had previously been arrested in 2024 and 2025 at demonstrations, including one outside the Israeli consulate at which he allegedly set fire to Israeli and American flags. He is still awaiting trial for those incidents.

The blast killed Bartkus, damaged buildings, and injured four other people. An accomplice, Daniel Park, was later charged with providing and attempting to provide material support to a terrorist. Park killed himself in custody in June 2025. Evidence uncovered in the wake of the attack suggested that Bartkus subscribed to a fringe belief system known as pro-mortalism, a nihilistic philosophy which argues that life primarily consists of suffering and that humans should die in order to prevent future suffering. White instead drove across the street to a pharmacy and from there opened fire at the CDC headquarters, firing almost 200 shots. He also shot and killed a responding police officer, David Rose of the DeKalb County Police Department, before using one of the five firearms he brought with him to kill himself. According to authorities and people who knew the shooter, White had expressed anti-vaccine sentiments and conspiracy theories and believed that the COVID-19 vaccine had affected his mental state.

Audit/HEAT Map Text: Hassan M. Muse was arrested by police following a deadly shooting in front of the Portland Central Library. The victim, Douglas Ivers, was taken to a hospital where he was declared dead. According to prosecutors, Muse got into an argument with the victim, who pulled out a can of bear spray and pointed it at Muse before turning to walk away. Muse then allegedly took a handgun from a shopping bag and shot the victim in the back, then again when he was on the ground. In court for his arraignment on charges of second-degree murder and unlawful use of a weapon, Muse declared that he was a "sovereign political power holder," suggesting that he considered himself a sovereign citizen. As of this writing, police have not made clear a possible motive.

Vance Boelter allegedly killed Minnesota State Representative Melissa Hortman and her husband, shooting them in their home while dressed as a law enforcement officer. In a similar fashion, Boelter also allegedly shot a state senator, John Hoffman, and his wife; those two victims survived. He visited the homes of two other officials, but they were not present at the time. Police officers arrived at Hortman's home, the last house targeted by Boelter, while Boelter was still there. One of the officers fired at Boelter but did not hit him, and Boelter escaped. He was captured nearly two days later after an extensive manhunt. Boelter faces state first-degree murder and attempted murder charges as well as numerous federal charges. All the targets that night were Democrats. According to law enforcement, Boelter had a hit list in his car that included politicians as well as individuals with connections to abortion providers or abortion rights advocacy. Boelter allegedly texted his wife that he "went to war." Described by the FBI as a survivalist, Boelter was also reportedly heavily religious, with charismatic beliefs tied to what some have characterized as "Christian Nationalism." According to a friend and roommate, Boelter was a devotee of conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and believed that civil war would erupt if Kamala Harris won the 2024 election.

Audit/HEAT Map Text: On or about November 23, 2021, Daniel Blanks and Reginald Baker forced their way into an apartment in Springdale, Arkansas, and beat its occupant, Richard Phillips, unconscious. According to law enforcement, the attack stemmed from accusations that Phillips had sexually abused a child. The two men dragged Phillips down the stairs and into the back of a pickup truck, taking his body to the Mark Twain National Forest in Missouri, where Blanks allegedly shot him multiple times. His body was found by hunters some days later. The two assailants were arrested and charged in Arkansas with capital murder, kidnapping and residential burglary. Blanks was also charged federally; he subsequently pleaded guilty to federal charges of aiding and abetting kidnapping resulting in death. As of April 2025, he had not yet been tried on the state charges. A federal judge sentenced Blanks to life in prison without parole, citing as an aggravating factor his affiliation with white supremacist groups. Baker pleaded guilty in 2024 to state charges of accomplice to murder in the first degree, accomplice to kidnapping and accomplice to residential burglary; he received a sentence of 60 years.

Federal prosecutors charged Kadin Hawkeye Lewis with possession of unregistered destructive devices, attempted malicious use of fire and explosives and carrying explosives during the commission of a felony, all related to an alleged plot by Lewis to commit a mass casualty attack. The arrest stemmed from a homicide investigation that began in September 2022 when a body with gunshot wounds was discovered in a trailer belonging to Lewis. The corpse was later identified as Casey Anderson. Police said that in addition to the body, they found writings and drawings with white supremacist symbols and references. A journal allegedly detailed a plan to commit a mass casualty event inspired by previous school shooters. Police also allegedly found a number of Molotov cocktails and the components for more such incendiary devices. Local authorities charged Lewis with homicide, but in July 2024, asked the court to dismiss the charges without prejudice because they did not feel they had enough evidence to convict Lewis at that time. However, in the federal case against Lewis, prosecutors have alleged that the murder "was part of Lewis's ultimate plan to carry out an attack."

In late February 2025, sheriff's deputies performing a wellness check at a residence found the bodies of Donald Mayer and Tatiana Casap, who had been shot to death on or around February 11. Wisconsin officials charged him with two counts of intentional first-degree homicide and other crimes. In April, the FBI claimed in court filings that authorities found on Nikita Casap's phone a short manifesto with accelerationist white supremacist rhetoric calling for the assassination of President Donald Trump in order to start a revolution and "save the white race" from politicians controlled by Jews. The FBI also said the murders appeared to be a way to obtain the money needed to carry out his plans. Authorities say that Casap had been in touch with members of The Order of Nine Angles, a neo-Nazi Satanist group. Casap also allegedly paid for a drone and explosives to be used for an attack. Joshua Jahn opened fire with a rifle at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) building from a nearby rooftop, spraying the building, parking lot, and vehicles with what police described as "indiscriminate" fire. Multiple shots hit an ICE van parked at the facility that contained detainees, hitting three of them, one fatally. A second detainee died of the wounds he sustained several days later. Jahn also fatally shot himself during the incident. Authorities later found notes at his home that they characterized as "anti-ICE." The full contents of Jahn's writings have not been made public, but authorities claim that one of them referred to ICE employees as "people showing up to collect a dirty paycheck." They have also said that another note hoped the attack "will give ICE agents real terror" and make them wonder about future snipers. Authorities have also claimed that one of the bullets found at the scene had "anti-ICE" scrawled on it.

Stefan Day Rowold set fire to a church belonging to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, vandalizing it and setting fire to religious books and paintings in an attempt to burn the building down. When the building was not destroyed, he returned three days later and set fire to it again, seriously damaging it. Rowold confessed to police, telling them that LDS members were evil and that they engaged in polygamy and child molestation. In September 2025, Rowold was convicted on state charges of arson, damaging religious property and use of fire to commit a felony.

On the evening of May 29-30, 2020, Colinford Mattis and Urooj Rahman, both attorneys, attended protests at a police precinct in the wake of the death of George Floyd. They brought materials with them to make Molotov cocktails; Rahman tried to convince other protesters to use them. She then threw an incendiary device at a parked police vehicle, setting it on fire. The two were later indicted on federal counts of arson, use of explosives and civil disorder, among other charges. Both eventually pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit arson, with Mattis receiving one year in prison and Rahman a 15-month sentence. Both were also subsequently disbarred.

The most serious incidents occurred on August 26, when group members unsuccessfully attempted to use a Molotov cocktail against police vehicles; on August 28, when members again threw Molotov cocktails against police vehicles, destroying one; and on September 3, when they went to North Little Rock and used a Molotov cocktail to destroy a police vehicle belonging to that city's police department. Federal authorities later charged the five on numerous counts, including conspiracy to commit arson, arson and possession of unregistered destructive devices. The defendants all pleaded guilty during 2022-2023, receiving sentences from 17 months to 66 months in prison.
